chunks: As for what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated, from Ibn Sinān, from Ibn Muskān, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said:

I asked him about performing wudu (ablution) from water into which a dog had lapped, or a cat, or from which a camel or a riding animal or something else had drunk: may wudu (ablution) be performed from it, or ghusl? He said: “Yes, unless you find other than it, then avoid it.”

So there is no concession in this report regarding that in which a dog has lapped, because what is intended by it is when it exceeds the kurr amount which does not admit impurity; and that which indicates this is as follows.

key_terms.الْكَلْبُ: the dog, whose contact here is discussed in relation to water purity
key_terms.الْكُرِّ: the measure of kurr, a large quantity of water in fiqh that is not easily affected by najasah
key_terms.الْوُضُوءِ: wudu (ablution), the ritual washing before salat (prayer)
key_terms.رُخْصَةٌ: a concession or allowance in the legal ruling
key_terms.وَلَغَ: lapped with the tongue, especially said of an animal drinking from water
key_terms.يُغْتَسَلُ: ghusl is performed, meaning ritual bathing with the water

ai.seo_question: Can wudu (ablution) or ghusl be performed with water from which a dog or other animals have drunk?
ai.summary: This hadith addresses the ruling of using water for wudu (ablution) or ghusl after animals have drunk from it. It indicates permissibility in general, while the accompanying clarification explains that the case of a dog is understood in relation to a large quantity of water reaching the measure of kurr, which is not rendered impure by such contact.
